preamble: Eight solutions, not further defined, complete the intro.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ask Woody Allen, woodwind wallah, to play song's intro

indicators.note: to play with letters is to toss them about freely, so these names and words get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the first part of the letters to be rearranged
taken as written; a wallah is a person employed in a given job, here a woodwind player

explanation.surface: A request to the clarinet-playing film-maker Woody Allen to strike up the opening of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: All twenty-seven letters of the fodder are used; Woody Allen famously plays jazz clarinet, a woodwind, which makes the surface apt. The answer runs across three lights.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's nonsense song opens with the line about an old lady swallowing a fly, so these words are its opening.

clue.text: "I think it's OK at sea, barring hits", an adventurer wrote

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the book the explorer Thor Heyerdahl wrote

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the remaining letters are jumbled
barring means excluding, so the letters of the word hits are struck out of the phrase

parts.note: taken as written, the phrase whose letters are worked on

explanation.surface: Someone sailing the ocean says things are fine as long as no collisions occur, quoted from an explorer's account.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'hits' (H, I, T, S) are struck out of the opening phrase, the H apart from the other three, and what is left is rearranged. Heyerdahl's raft voyage was told in his book of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Kon-Tiki is the 1948 account by Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl of his raft voyage, so it is a book written by an adventurer.

clue.text: Not all accoutrements are off the wall

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the next word are used, so the answer lies hidden within it

parts.note: taken as written, the word containing the answer

explanation.surface: Some accessories are bizarre, says someone eyeing a wardrobe.
explanation.definitionFit: Outré describes something unconventional or bizarre, which is what off-the-wall means as an idiom.

clue.text: A nurse in charge guards rare poison

indicators.note: to guard is to stand round something, so the outer letters enclose the next piece

parts.note: taken as written
SEN is a State Enrolled Nurse, an older British nursing grade
R is a recognised abbreviation for rare, as on a steak order

explanation.surface: A senior nurse on duty is protecting a scarce toxic substance on the ward.
explanation.walkthrough: SEN stands for State Enrolled Nurse, a grade formerly used in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenic is a notoriously lethal element, the classic murderer's choice in detective fiction.

clue.text: See 1
PC likely to staunch cut

indicators.note: staunching a wound means plugging it, so this word sits inside the other

parts.note: to lop is to cut off
apt means likely or inclined, as in apt to rain

explanation.surface: A police constable is apparently going to stop a bleeding wound.
explanation.walkthrough: PC looks like police constable; it is the personal computer.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal computer, the common example of a PC.

clue.text: Prepare to ambush 27 with heavy object to the ear

indicators.note: as heard rather than read, so the pieces are spoken and the sound written differently

parts.note: the answer to 27 across, a big cat
a weight is a heavy object, as on scales or in a gym

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to a big cat stalking its prey, plus something heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 27 across answer said with a heavy object gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie in wait is to stay hidden ready to spring an attack, the idiom for preparing an ambush.

clue.text: Ruminants slip on leather, falling over

indicators.note: in a down clue something falling over is turned upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: to skid is to slip
kid is soft leather made from young goatskin

explanation.surface: Someone slips on a leather surface and tumbles.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Dik-diks are small African antelopes, and antelopes chew the cud like cattle.

clue.text: See 1 across
Good article in good books

indicators.note: the article is placed inside the letters for good and good books

parts.note: NT is the New Testament, books of the Good Book

explanation.surface: A worthy grammatical article finds itself in someone's good books.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's FLY. 'In good books' looks like an idiom for favour; NT is the New Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; a gnat is a small two-winged insect, so it stands for the fly the old lady swallowed.

clue.text: School president hosts very subdued monarch

definitions.text: School president hosts very subdued monarch

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the president's name holds the next letters

parts.note: Ike was the nickname of US President Eisenhower
PP, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quiet
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the monarch's cipher

explanation.surface: A school head entertains a very quiet king or queen.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's DOG. Ike was President Eisenhower's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; the schipperke is a small black Belgian breed, originally a barge dog, standing for the dog in the song.

clue.text: Perhaps sow one ground

parts.note: a sow is one example of a pig, signalled by Perhaps

indicators.note: ground means crushed or milled, so the letters of one are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Maybe someone scatters seed on a single patch of land.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's BIRD. 'Sow' looks like a verb about seed but is the female pig.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; a pigeon is a common plump grey bird, standing for the bird the old lady swallowed.

clue.text: Mollusc eating weed as sole security?

definitions.note: a fanciful phrase for a nail that fastens a shoe's sole

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside, so the mollusc holds the next piece

parts.note: a snail is a mollusc
to hoe is to weed

explanation.surface: A garden snail munches weeds, perhaps the only safeguard a gardener has.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sole' looks like 'only'; it is the bottom of a shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoenail is a nail used in shoemaking to fix the sole firmly, so it keeps the sole secure.

clue.text: Stop working with artist said to be regime changer?

definitions.note: a jokey description of someone who alters people's diet regimes

parts.note: a machine that dies stops working

indicators.note: said means spoken aloud, so the painter's name is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Titian was the Venetian Renaissance painter

explanation.surface: Someone quits work to be with an artist, which is called a political upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regime change' suggests politics; the regime is a diet.
explanation.definitionFit: A dietician plans and alters people's eating plans, so they change dietary regimes for a living.

clue.text: Pavlova, for one, reacted on being whipped

indicators.note: whipping beats something into a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A meringue dessert reacted when cream was whipped for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Pavlova looks like the dessert of whipped cream and meringue; it is Anna Pavlova, the ballerina who gave it her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna Pavlova was a Russian ballerina who danced en pointe, so she is a famous example of a toe dancer.

clue.text: Every so often draw in Skye

definitions.text: Every so often draw in Skye

indicators.note: only some letters at regular gaps are used, here every other one

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be picked from

explanation.surface: From time to time someone sketches on the Scottish isle of Skye.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's COW, Daisy being a traditional name for one. Skye is an island off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; Daisy is the stock name for a dairy cow in nursery tales, so it stands for the cow.

clue.text: Fancied player gains lead in tennis

definitions.text: Fancied player gains lead in tennis

indicators.note: to gain is to take something in, so the player holds the next letter

parts.note: a seed is a player ranked high in a tournament draw

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written, the word whose first letter is used

explanation.surface: A top-ranked player goes in front in a tennis match.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's HORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; steed is a literary word for a riding mount, so it stands for the horse in the song.

clue.text: Three notes for two from treble and tenor

parts.note: treble means three times, the same as triple
T for tenor in vocal scores

explanation.surface: A choir arranges a passage for treble and tenor voices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treble' looks like a voice part; it means threefold.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a triplet is a group of three notes played in the time normally taken by two.

clue.text: Open trophy ultimately kept in county jail

indicators.note: the final letter is placed inside the county and jail letters

parts.note: Clare is a county in the west of Ireland
jug is slang for prison

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of kept is used

parts.note: taken as written, the word whose last letter is used

explanation.surface: A golf trophy has finally ended up locked away in a local prison.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open is the British Open golf championship. Clare is an Irish county; jug is slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: The Claret Jug is the silver trophy presented to the winner of golf's Open Championship.

clue.text: New York street eclipsing British one

definitions.note: stands for a street, picking up the street of the wordplay

indicators.note: to eclipse is to blot out, so the letter is removed from the street name

parts.note: Broadway is the famous avenue running the length of Manhattan

explanation.surface: A famous Manhattan avenue outshines a British high street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eclipsing' looks like outdoing; it means wiping out B. 'One' refers back to a street.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadway is the part of a road used by traffic, so it is a kind of street.

clue.text: Drives out superior special troops

parts.note: U is the old label for upper-class, superior usage

indicators.note: special forces are irregular troops, and here the word marks the letters as rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A senior officer leads elite special forces.
explanation.walkthrough: U is short for upper class, a British usage made famous by Nancy Mitford's U and non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot people is to force them from their homes, so it means to drive them out.

clue.text: Phone left in literary lady's bedroom

indicators.note: the letter for left goes inside the old word for a lady's room

parts.note: a bower is a poetic word for a lady's private chamber

explanation.surface: A phone has been left in a lady's chamber in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The blower is British slang for the telephone.
explanation.definitionFit: Blower is informal British slang for the telephone, as in 'get on the blower'.

clue.text: Ban papers backing everyone in broadcast

indicators.note: going backwards, so the letters for papers are read in reverse

parts.note: ID means identity papers

indicators.note: everyone is placed inside the word for broadcast

parts.note: to sow seed is to scatter or broadcast it
all means everyone

explanation.surface: A regulator bans newspapers that support everybody in a radio or TV programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like radio or TV; it means scattering seed.
explanation.definitionFit: To disallow something is to refuse to allow it, which is the same as banning it.

clue.text: A new artist saves energy

indicators.note: the artist saves energy as in keeping it in front, so the artist's letters follow

parts.note: taken as written
go means energy or vigour
RA, Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A newcomer painter is economical with power.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's GOAT, a long-haired breed. RA is a Royal Academician.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; the Angora is a Turkish breed of domestic goat whose fleece gives mohair, standing for the goat.

clue.text: Information about a liberal physician

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the information letters are wrapped around the next piece

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
taken as written

explanation.surface: Details concerning a doctor of liberal politics.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Galen was the celebrated Greek physician of the Roman Empire whose medical teaching dominated for centuries.

clue.text: Boycott wives defending union response

parts.note: to black something is to boycott it, a trade-union term

indicators.note: defenders surround what they protect, so the wives' letters stand either side

parts.note: W for wife, doubled for the plural
I do is the response made at a wedding, a union

explanation.surface: Wives refusing to cross a picket line still stand up for the trade union's answer.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's SPIDER. 'Union' looks like a trade union; it is marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; the black widow is a venomous arachnid, standing for the spider the old lady swallowed.

clue.text: Large one running

parts.note: L for large, as on clothes
I is the Roman numeral one
on means working or running, as of a machine

explanation.surface: A big contestant in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the eight undefined theme answers: it is the song's CAT, a big one.
explanation.definitionFit: As a theme answer it has no definition; the lion is the great African big cat, standing for the cat the old lady swallowed.

clue.text: Cooler fish dish

parts.note: cooler and stir are both slang for prison
fry are young fish

explanation.surface: A cold-store fish course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' looks like something colder; it is slang for jail.
explanation.definitionFit: A stir-fry is a quickly cooked dish of chopped food tossed in a wok.

clue.text: My 10s flummoxed athlete on horse

indicators.note: flummoxed means baffled and thrown, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the plural of the 10 across answer

explanation.surface: Someone's little flies baffled a rider.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse is the vaulting apparatus, not an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnast performs routines on the pommel or vaulting horse, a piece of gym apparatus.
